articles.title: Trump's stunning 'fever dream' animating his latest 'astonishingly brazen' scheme: expert
articles.description: A legal expert shredded the "fever dream" that seems to be animating President Donald Trump's latest push to limit birthright citizenship. Harry Litman, a former federal prosecutor, argued in a new essay on his Substack, "Talking Feds," that Trump's new executive order, which creates new exceptions for birthright citizenship and places limits on so-called "birth tourism," is destined to fail at the Supreme Court. He described the move as another iteration of Trump's "favorite play" — taking a loss and calling it a win — that revealed the president hasn't grasped how resoundingly the Supreme Court rejected him the last time he tried this scheme. "It’s a fever dream," Litman wrote. "The chief order directly conflicts with Barbara , and it is destined to fail the first time the administration tries to use it. The second is subtler, and its fate will depend on how it’s administered." Litman was referring to the case Trump v. Barbara , in which the Supreme Court held that Trump's previous executive order ending birthright citizenship flew in the face of the 14th Amendment. Since then, Trump has lashed out at the Supreme Court by accusing it of costing the country "trillions" of dollars because of the ruling. Trump officials like Stephen Miller, deputy chief of staff, and Will Scharf, the new White House counsel, have also repeated false claims about the legality of the order, Litman noted. For instance, he pointed to Miller's "astonishingly brazen" claim that the 14th Amendment was written to guarantee citizenship to the children of slaves, a claim that the Supreme Court explicitly rejected, Litman noted. Litman was also taken aback by Scharf's claim that nothing in the new executive order “runs afoul of any of the Supreme Court’s opinions." Litman described the claim as "stunning that the Trump administration would claim with a straight face."

articles.title: Mir Raza’s grave is not a silent one
articles.description: There is a particular cruelty in a name being spoken twice by death. Once when it is buried. And once when it is dug up again, because the truth could not rest with it. Mir Raza, the son of Mir Hassan Ali Khan, and Wafflix business owner, was laid into the earth of Rehorania Masjid graveyard on the 29th of July. Eleven days later, a board of doctors, a police surgeon, a magistrate, and a family that refused to let silence be the final word stood over that same soil and opened it again. I have read the report. I do not think I will ever be able to unread it. It is written in the flat, careful language that medicine keeps for what it cannot otherwise bear to say. Somewhere inside that distance is a twenty-five-year-old man who once had a face his mother could recognise without being told his name. What the doctors found confirmed what the family had feared all along, that Mir Raza did not simply die. He was taken from them. And when asked, plainly, whether his wounds came before death, someone circled a single word on the page: Yes . That word has not left me since. What stays with me most is not the injury itself, but the effort that surrounded it. The care taken. The insistence, even now, that this body still deserved to be handled gently, named properly, treated as someone rather than something. Dr Summaiya Syed, Police Surgeon of Karachi, stood at that graveside and did what very few of us are ever asked to do. She looked directly at what injustice leaves behind, and she did not turn away. There is a particular kind of courage in choosing, on an ordinary working day, to be the last honest witness a murdered man will ever have. It is not the courage of headlines. It is quieter than that, and heavier, and it asks everything of the stomach and the soul, and gives back only the satisfaction of having told the truth when it would have been so much easier not to. And yet, the final word on how Mir Raza died has still not been given. Not because there is doubt. The findings speak clearly enough. It has simply not been said out loud, in the way that matters, in the place that matters. Twelve days passed, the doctors believe, between his death and the moment anyone was able to examine him. Twelve days in which a family did not know. And then more days still, in which even his grave had to be argued for, before the truth was allowed to be looked at a second time. We spend our lives pretending we are not what that grave revealed. We make plans, we argue over small things, we behave as though we will always have tomorrow to fix what we said today. But strip away the years, and every one of us ends the same way Mir Raza did. Plain. Unrecognisable, even to those who loved us most. If that is where we are all headed, then what exactly are we fighting for when we fight for justice? I do not think it is the body. The earth takes that regardless. I think it is the truth of what was done to someone while they were still here to feel it. That is the only part of us that does not decay. It is the only inheritance a murdered man can leave behind that no grave is deep enough to bury. Karachi did not let this one go quiet. Somewhere between a graveyard and a courtroom, ordinary people, neighbours, strangers, a city that has buried too many of its sons without asking enough questions, decided that Mir Raza’s silence was not going to be mistaken for peace. They spoke. They kept speaking, until an order was signed and a grave that should have been the end of his story became instead the place where it finally began to be told properly. That is not a small thing. In a country where so many cases are allowed to fade as quietly as a body returns to the earth, the refusal of ordinary citizens to look away is very often the only justice the dead will ever be given. So I find myself asking the only question I have left. If the truth has already been found, plainly, and written down, and confirmed by a circled word on a page, then what are we still waiting for? Where does justice go, in the space between a death and its acknowledgment? And where, in a city that loved this man loudly enough to bring him back up into the light so his story could be told rightly, does our humanity actually stand today? Not in the vigils. Not in the slogans. But in the quiet, unglamorous work of finishing what we started for Mir Raza. I do not have that answer yet. I am not sure any of us do. But I know this much. A city that will not let its dead be forgotten has not yet forgotten itself. And whatever else remains unresolved, that much still holds true: somewhere beneath all our exhaustion and all our grief, we still believe a man’s name is worth saying twice. Header image: Mir Raza Ali, a 25-year-old business owner whose body was found in bushes in Karachi’s Gulistan-i-Jauhar on July 29, following which a police probe into his death is ongoing. — Instagram/Wafflix

articles.title: Prime suspect in Rs8.5bn Yellow Line graft case under NAB scrutiny
articles.description: KARACHI: The legal troubles of the prime suspect in the Rs8.5 billion Yellow Line graft case, Zameer Abbasi, have further increased as the National Accountability Bureau (NAB) has initiated an inquiry into his alleged possession of assets beyond his known sources of income and his alleged “illegal appointments” or “promotions in the Sindh government”. Earlier in June, the Anti-Corruption Establishment (ACE) Sindh had booked Abbasi, the then project director of the Karachi Mobility Project (KMP), and others following an inquiry into alleged financial mismanagement in the KMP related to the Yellow Line. The inquiry committee report stated that Abbasi and then director procurement Jhaman made Rs8.5bn advance payments to contractors without bank guarantees despite the fact that their contracts lacked any specific clause regarding “advance payment and financial assistance to the contractors”. A source told Dawn that the NAB had initiated an inquiry against the senior bureaucrat over allegations of possessing assets beyond his known sources of income and illegal appointments or promotions in the Sindh government. Bureau seeks details of Zameer Abbasi’s assets, ‘illegal’ appointments, promotions As part of the inquiry, the bureau has sought details of immovable properties registered in the names of Abbasi, his wife and children and other family members from the concerned departments. According to the source, Abbasi began his career with NAB and was later deputed to the Sindh police as a DSP. After a Supreme Court directive, he was repatriated to his parent department, the NAB, where he served until 2016. In the same year, he was appointed as a grade-17 section officer. The appointment was challenged before a court on allegations that it was made through irregularities and that he had also received an out-of-turn promotion, the source claimed. The source further alleged that Abbasi had also approached the court, contending that his colleagues who had joined service with him had already been promoted to grade 19. However, before the court could decide his petition, he was promoted to grade 19, the source claimed. In 2022, he was appointed to another key position, but the appointment was challenged before a court, which suspended the notification. Although he subsequently disappeared from the public spotlight for some time, he was later appointed to another important position, the source added. The ACE only managed to apprehend Abbasi, a grade-19 officer of the Sindh government, claiming that he was arrested in Lahore and later produced him before the court concerned in Karachi. The provincial anti-corruption court also rejected his post-arrest bail application. Published in Dawn, August 10th, 2026
